headlines.title: Delta Air Lines cuts 2026 forecast on fuel surge, but CEO says demand is still strong
headlines.summary: Delta Air Lines reported third-quarter earnings and missed Wall Street estimates for the first time in two years.
headlines.article_text: Delta Air Lines (DAL) Q3 2026 earnings Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Delta Air Lines missed Wall Street earnings estimates for the first time in two years and cut its 2026 profit forecast. Delta CEO Ed Bastian said demand remains strong and that fares appear to be rising further as fuel prices stay high. Jet fuel prices have surged this year since the Iran war started in February, driving up airlines' second-largest cost after labor. In this article DAL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 6:07 06:07 Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian on Q3 results: We maintained our overall level of profitability Squawk Box Delta Air Lines slashed its 2026 profit outlook as high fuel prices persist, but CEO Ed Bastian said higher fares aren't turning off travelers. Delta on Friday forecast full-year earnings per share of between $5.10 and $5.60 on an adjusted basis, compared with its outlook in July, when fuel prices were lower, of $6.50 to $7.50 a share. The company's fourth-quarter guidance was below analyst estimates, too. Delta cut its free cash flow outlook for the year to $2.5 billion, from as much as $4 billion it expected in July. Still, Bastian said in an interview that fares have continued to tick up as the airline passes along much of a $6 billion increase in fuel costs this year, and that travelers keep booking. Jet fuel prices in the U.S. Gulf of Mexico region have almost doubled to $4.34 on Thursday from $2.19 a year earlier, according to FactSet. "The consumer response continues to be quite strong. We're seeing it across all channels, all cabins of service, all geographies, business, leisure," he said. Delta forecast a 20% increase in revenue for the fourth quarter over the same period last year, more than the 16% rise in the third quarter, when adjusting for the airline's benefit from its refinery in Trainer, Pennsylvania, where it refines crude oil into jet fuel and other products, giving it an advantage over other carriers. "Obviously the fuel pricing, the volatility of fuel prices have something to do with that," Bastian said. Delta is the country's most profitable airline and the first to report results from the third quarter, which encompasses the busy summer season. Costs continued to weigh on the bottom line. The fuel price surge since the Iran war began in February has put a damper on airline profits even as carriers flex pricing power. The latest inflation read in September showed airfare up more than 23% from a year earlier. Here's what the company reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on consensus estimates from LSEG: Earnings per share: $1.72 adjusted vs. $1.75 expected Adjusted revenue: $17.59 billion adjusted vs. $17.67 billion expected Delta reported net income of $756 million, or $1.15 a share, down 47% from $1.42 billion, or $2.17 per share, a year earlier. Adjusting for one-time items, Delta posted earnings of $1.76 per share. Adjusting for sales from its refinery, maintenance business and profit-sharing, revenue rose 16% from the previous year to $17.59 billion. Operating revenue jumped 21% in the third quarter to $20.19 billion. Delta's premium revenue, which has become a larger portion of its total sales, grew 18% in the third quarter to $6.82 billion, while main cabin sales rose only 12% to $6.8 billion. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk criticized Bastian on X last week, saying the Delta CEO would "lose his job over this" after the View from the Wing travel blog said Bastian told staff at an internal event "We do not want to be with Elon Musk. Trust me." SpaceX's Starlink Wi-Fi has become the main supplier of satellite Wi-Fi, with airline partnerships that include United Airlines , American Airlines , Southwest Airlines and Alaska Airlines , as well as others around the world. Delta's Bastian brushed off the idea of a personal spat with Musk on Friday and told CNBC's Phil LeBeau in an interview that "everyone's entitled to their opinion." "There's no tit-for-tat as far as I'm concerned," Bastian said. headlines.article_text: Ferrari’s chairman is bullish on AI. He’s less certain on monetization Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Ferrari chairman John Elkann has rejected concerns about an AI bubble, telling CNBC that a market correction will not derail the technology’s long-term progress. He acknowledged risks stemming from a mismatch between soaring AI infrastructure investment and uncertainty over business revenues. The industrialist told CNBC that European tech companies have the capability to compete with U.S. and Chinese rivals. In this article BSP RACE STLA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 4:41 04:41 Ferrari chair: I'm not an AI bubble believer Squawk Box Europe Ferrari chairman John Elkann has shrugged off concerns about a potential artificial intelligence bubble — but he warns an AI supply and demand mismatch could pose a risk to markets. In an exclusive interview with CNBC Friday, the billionaire industrialist and Meta Platforms board member, who has invested in technology companies through his family's holding company Exor, expressed optimism for the AI buildout in the decade ahead. Elkann, who is also chairman of auto multinational Stellantis , said the energy and compute requirements for AI-enabled technologies remains high. "What is less certain is what are the revenue-generating mechanisms and business models out of that technology," he said. "That's where you need to see where the mismatch can happen." Elkann said there were different types of bubbles, ranging from those driven purely by financial speculation to those fueled by a rapid buildup of investment and infrastructure. But he said investor focus should remain squarely on the technology's direction of travel. "I am not in the camp of the bubble believers," he said. "Again, I don't think ultimately bubbles, or bursts of bubbles, are going to be an impediment to what progress is, and how it is happening." Speaking to CNBC's Carolin Roth on the sidelines of this year's Wave 2026 technology conference in Turin — formerly known as Italian Tech Week — Elkann said European companies can offer "incredible technical capabilities," amid the increasingly fierce tech battle between the U.S. and China. "The opportunity set ultimately determines where investors will want to go," he observed of the prevailing investment landscape in the continent. "The more opportunities you have, the more capital will come to those opportunities." He highlighted Milan-headquartered conglomerate Bending Spoons — owner of Vimeo, Eventbrite and AOL, among others — as a "perfect example of how one company born in Italy can actually have global ambition, and be able to grow and compete in many different markets as they are doing." He added: "The more of these companies we have, the more will end up having investors backing them."
